description: Discovery flags for the Call Copilot. During discovery, when the prospect says something that should be dug into, the app surfaces the flag + the exact probe question. Built from Cole Gordon's discovery methodology (the 7 beliefs: pain, doubt, cost, desire, money, support, trust).

pain: What's the single biggest challenge in the business right now? Or what's not working at the level it truly could be?
Tell me more — when you said [that], what do you mean exactly? Why do you say that though?
Has that put you in a tough position? In what way? How's it showing up day to day?

Take me back to the LAST time you tried to fix this -- what specifically happened? What did it cost you? (Past-pain probe -- Jeremy Miner. Past-pain auto-generates future-fear: their brain projects 'this will happen again' without you having to say it. More powerful than 'what if nothing changes' because the emotion is already loaded.)
doubt: Before we met today, were you out there looking for other potential solutions to [their problem]? ... [they name a past attempt] Hold on — how do you mean it didn't work out? (Jeremy Miner solution-awareness wrapper. Sets up the past-pain probe + re-meaning + identity-shift chain naturally — ask BEFORE the past-pain probe so the prospect surfaces the failed attempt themselves rather than you fishing for it.)
What have you already tried to fix this? What happened?
When something like that doesn't work, it's usually one of two things — the method or the execution. Which do you think it was?
What's been the single biggest thing keeping you from fixing this on your own?
cost: Can I ask you another personal question — and I really hate to ask this — but what's your plan if nothing changes? What if the last five years are like the next five years? (Cole, Batch 3:105 / Batch 4:143 — exact verbatim.)
If we roll forward 12 months and the business is still exactly here, what does that actually cost you — money, time, energy?
What's it costing you right now to keep going the way you are?
desire: Where do you want the business to be? What's the revenue number you're driving toward, and why that number specifically?
What would hitting that actually let you do — personally — that you can't do right now?
Is there any other reason this is important to you now though?
money: Just for clarity — what was your exact revenue last month? And the month before?
What's a single client worth to you over their lifetime?
If this is the right move, is the budget there to make it happen — or would you need to free something up?
support: Who else is involved in a decision like this?
Is your partner supportive of you making this change? Do they know you're on this call — what would they think if they knew?
If your team has to implement this, do they have the bandwidth this quarter?

(no-fly surface — Charlie Platt loss) When you mentioned [their language — e.g. 'we as a couple', 'we plan together', 'our 5-year plan'], it sounds like your partner is part of how decisions like this get made. Tell me how that usually plays out when you make a big call like this — do you decide and inform, or genuinely decide together?
(open partner-tonight probe — Cole, Batch 8): When you go talk to them tonight, what are you going to tell them about what we discussed?
trust: What would make you 100% confident that we're the team to get you there?
Have you looked at other options? What's drawing you to look at this now?
Is there anything about working with us specifically you're unsure of — so I can clear it up now?
math: What's a single client worth to you over their lifetime?
On average, how many clients do you close a month?
What's your current monthly revenue? And what would you need it to be? (Lock these — they're the inputs to the conservative upside math at committing.)
why: What's the REAL reason they want to make this change RIGHT NOW — not the surface goal?

If they had to write the why on a sticky note in one sentence, what would it actually say? (And does it sound like something they'd say to a stranger, or only to someone close — the latter means the mask is off.)
People don't book a call for no reason (Cole). What shifted recently that made NOW the time? What happened?

flags.signal: Vague or surface-level answer — they haven't really told you anything yet
flags.probe: Tell me more — when you said [that], what do you mean exactly? Why do you say that though?
flags.note: Don't move on. Paint the full portrait — repeat their last 3 words back as a question to get them to expand.

flags.signal: They used an emotional word — there's real pain here, go deeper
flags.probe: Tell me more about that. Has that put you in a tough position? ... In what way though? How's that showing up for you?
flags.note: Emotional words are gold — chase them. Get to the real, personal cost, not the surface.

flags.signal: They named a specific goal/number — find out why THAT number
flags.probe: You seem like you've thought of that number before — can I ask, why that number? Why is that important to you? When do you want to hit it by?
flags.note: A number with no 'why' behind it is shallow. Anchor it.

flags.signal: They mentioned a spouse/partner — FLAG support; qualify it now, don't handle it
flags.probe: Is your partner supportive of you fixing this? Are you guys on the same page about that problem? Does your partner know you're on this call — and what would they think if they knew?
flags.note: Gather it now, naturally — do NOT handle a spouse objection in discovery. You'll need this later.

flags.signal: They said 'we' / 'us' / 'the team' — there may be other decision-makers
flags.probe: When you say 'we' — who else is involved in a decision like this? Who would need to be comfortable with it if we decided it's the right move?
flags.note: Surface every decision-maker early. A hidden one kills the close.

flags.signal: They've tried something before — run solution questions, set up the pitch
flags.probe: What did you like or dislike about it? What was missing? When people go into something like that and don't get the result, it's usually one of two things — the method, or the execution. Which do you think it was?
flags.note: This is your ammo. The pitch must explain why that failed and why this is different.

flags.signal: They gave a goal but not the real reason behind it
flags.probe: Why is that important to you? Why now though? And seeing as you're the founder — why is that important to you personally?
flags.note: Use permission-reason-why for the deep personal reason: 'Can I ask a personal question? The reason I'm asking is...'

flags.signal: They've been stuck a long time — find the moment of decision
triggers: as long as i can remember
flags.probe: Take me back to the last day you had that sudden realization that enough is enough — the day you decided to draw the line in the sand, step across it, burn the boats. Take me back to that day — what actually happened?
flags.note: The moment of decision resurfaces the emotions of change. This is the highest-leverage discovery question.

flags.signal: They're downplaying, or money / pain isn't a lever — no clear problem surfaced
triggers: i don't really have a problem
flags.probe: On a scale of one to ten, where's [their area] at right now? ... And what does that number mean to you? ... If pain / money clearly isn't the lever (Matt Ryder): people don't book a call for no reason — what shifted recently that made NOW the time to look at this? Have you tried anything before, and why didn't it stick? Then measure the gap: how close does your current way realistically get you to [their goal]?
flags.note:
No problem, no sale. If the prospect downplays, run the 1-10 gap question. If they say money / pain isn't the issue, switch to the catalyst-event line — there is always a reason they got on the call; the gap between their current method and their goal IS the urgency.

If they're a HIGH-REVENUE / no-pain prospect (Cole): you're not building from pain, you're building from unfulfilled desire. Playful disarm FIRST: 'we never have companies come to us wanting to learn how to sell less -- they always want to learn how to sell more. Is that why you came to us?' Then build the gap forward: 'if we came in and did [X], where do you FEEL you could get in 12 months?' (verbal pace + 'feel' to keep them emotional). If they lob a humble number, call it: 'OK, 15 -- is that your humble goal? You can tell me, we're not posting it on Instagram.'

SEQUENCING (Jeremy Miner): the 'we never have companies come to us wanting to sell less' line must be delivered PLAYFUL FIRST to disarm — then switch to serious/concerned. Lead with serious tone = guard goes up, prospect rejects the frame. Playful tone IS the disarm — not a vibe, a deliberate sequence. Triggers to add: 'sharpen our sword', 'sharpen the sword', 'always looking to improve', 'looking to improve'.

flags.signal: They're telling a story instead of giving you numbers
flags.probe: Got it — let's get specific. Last week exactly, how many [leads/calls/sales]? What about the week before? What was your exact revenue last month?
flags.note: People tell stories about their problems; the truth is in the numbers. Chunk down.

flags.signal: They mentioned a competitor or other option — FLAG, note it, don't chase now
flags.probe: (Note it — don't handle it in discovery.) Later, at the close: 'Price aside, which are you more certain can actually get you there?'
flags.note: Don't reframe in discovery. Flush it out, save it for the transition/objections.

flags.signal: They're pushing to price before discovery is done
flags.probe: Everything we do is customized — so the most time-efficient thing is to get a little context first, then I can share the parts relevant to you. Is that fair?
flags.note: Don't drop the price early. Redirect to discovery. Pricing before value = lost deal.

flags.signal: They asked a logistics question — there may be a hidden objection under it
triggers: do i get one on one
flags.probe: There are elements of [X] — but just so I can answer your question correctly, is there a specific reason you're asking?
flags.note: Never answer a logistics question flat. The reason behind it is usually the real objection.

flags.signal: They mentioned a deadline or external pressure — that's cost/urgency
triggers: by the end of the year
flags.probe: What happens if nothing changes? If we roll this forward 90 days and you're still dealing with the same thing — what gets harder, what stays off the table?
flags.note: This is the cost-of-inaction lever. Dig the consequence, then ladder deeper.

flags.signal: They're hedging — uncertainty you'll need to clear at the temp check
flags.probe: (Note the hedge.) At the temp check, push for certainty: 'Do you think this is 100% going to work? Do you 100% want to do this?'
flags.note: A hedge now becomes an objection at the close. Flag it.

flags.signal: The owner is stuck working IN the business — trapped in delivery / the day-to-day
triggers: stuck in the day to day
flags.probe: What would the business look like if you weren't in the day-to-day of it? ... If this freed you from [that part], what would you actually do with that time — and what would it mean for the business to run without you in the engine room?
flags.note: For a business owner the real desire is usually leverage — getting out of delivery, not out of a job. Tie the goal to what their time gets reinvested into.

flags.signal: They voiced a fear or risk — chase it now, it becomes the nerves objection later
flags.probe: Tell me more about that — what specifically worries you? Why do you say that though?
flags.note: A voiced fear in discovery is the doubt belief surfacing early. Chase the emotional word now to understand it — but don't fully HANDLE it as the nerves objection until the committing phase.

flags.signal: They mentioned kids/family/lifestyle — tie the goal to the personal payoff
flags.probe: Can I ask you a personal question? The reason I'm asking is we want this to work around your lifestyle goals — so what are the personal goals you want your business to allow you to achieve?
flags.note: The strongest sales tie the monetary goal to a non-monetary, personal one.

flags.signal: They contradicted something they said earlier — flag it for the loop
triggers: now that i think about it
flags.probe: (Note the contradiction.) Later: 'Earlier you said [X], but now you're saying [Y] — what's really going on?'
flags.note: Their own words are the most powerful tool to handle a later objection.

flags.signal: Long rambling answer — cut in, redirect, get specific
triggers: i don't know if that makes sense
flags.probe: Got it — let me make sure I understand. So the main thing is [their core point], right? Let's dig into that specifically.
flags.note: Don't let discovery sprawl. Stay in the lead, get to the gap.

flags.signal: They mentioned being busy / no time — probe priorities now, it'll become an objection later
flags.probe: If [their constraint] is the #1 thing holding the business back — why wouldn't fixing it be your #1 priority? If not now, when?
flags.note: Pre-empt the 'no time to implement' objection by anchoring priorities here.

flags.signal: They've named a problem — but make sure it's the REAL constraint
flags.probe: What do you think has been the biggest thing keeping you from fixing that on your own? What's in the way?
flags.note: Prospects often misdiagnose. Probe the real constraint before agreeing with their diagnosis.

flags.signal: They expressed doubt (or overconfidence) about doing it alone — the doubt belief
triggers: i could probably do it myself
i know what to do i just
flags.probe: If you could've done it on your own, you probably would have by now — so what's actually been in the way? What's been the hardest part?
flags.note: Address why a proven path beats DIY: less time, energy, and risk to the result.

flags.signal: They gave you a real reason — anchor it, then go one level deeper
triggers: what it really comes down to
flags.probe: I guess that makes sense — is there any other reason this is important to you now though?
flags.note: The 'any other reason' question often surfaces the truest, most emotional driver. Everyone has two reasons — the one that sounds good and the real one.

flags.signal: They mentioned money/cash being tight — install the money belief NOW, in discovery
flags.probe: Has that put you in a tough position financially — in what way though? ... Is that a revenue problem, or is it more about where the money's going right now?
flags.note: Surface and install the money belief in discovery — a financial-tightness comment now, left alone, becomes a price objection at the close. Installing the money belief in discovery creates the consistency that eliminates the financial objection later.

flags.signal: Long-running problem or a goal with no urgency — install the cost belief
flags.probe: Can I ask you another personal question — and I really hate to ask this — but what's your plan if nothing changes? What if the last five years are like the next five years?
flags.note: The cost-of-inaction lever. This is Cole's single most-repeated cost question — it makes the prospect feel the price of standing still.

flags.signal: They talk lead/revenue volume without qualifying fit — probe ICP quality
flags.probe: Out of those leads, how many actually fit the exact ideal client you want to attract? ... Let's get specific — what was your exact revenue last month? What about the month before? Is that gross or net?
flags.note: Chunk down to numbers. The real problem is often lead QUALITY, not volume — and stories hide it, numbers reveal it.

flags.signal: They used a ceiling word that reveals a low belief — catch it and reset
flags.probe: Can I make a suggestion on a word I just heard you say that could be holding us back? You said [their word] — have you ever thought that when we focus on getting [the least / the just / what we'd be happy with], what do we typically get? And you don't come across to me as the type of person who wants the least things in life. Would I be right? ... So what do you really want? (Jeremy Miner — identity-shift via word-catch.)
flags.note:
Jeremy Miner's word-catch move. Their first answer reveals their ceiling — flip it now before it caps the rest of the call. Use a concerned, soft tone — 'could be holding US back', never 'YOU back'. Never accuse.

COLE 3-STAGE REFRAME for 'at least' / 'I'd be happy with': (1) 'Can I make a suggestion on a word I heard that could be holding US back?' (US, not YOU — doesn't accuse). (2) 'You said the LEAST. Have you ever thought — when we focus on getting the least things in life, what do you typically get? ... The least.' (3) 'And you don't come across to me as the person who wants to get the least things in life. Would I be right?' (4) 'So what do you really want?' Belief surface → negative identity flip → re-anchor the real number. Don't skip to step 4.

flags.signal: They quoted revenue as an annual figure -- likely a one-good-month brag, not a real run rate
flags.probe: Got it -- and just based on last month specifically, what did you do? ... And the month before? (Cole: small biz owners quote 'about $1M/yr' then concede '$40k last month' -- the annual is the brag number, the monthly is the real one. Anchor the upside math to the monthly, not the annual.)
flags.note: If the monthly comes in <1/12 of the stated annual, it's the one-good-month tell. Pivot the rest of discovery off the real number. Saying nothing and accepting the annual figure means the upside math at committing is built on fiction.
